title: A Map Made by Walking
passage:
Nana's class received an unusual geography assignment. Instead of studying only a printed map, students had to walk around their neighborhood and create a map showing how the area felt to a person on foot. At first, Nana did not understand the difference. A normal map already showed roads, parks, and buildings. What else was there to record? Her group began by walking from the school to the public library. They soon noticed details that were missing from the printed map. One sidewalk became very narrow near a bridge. A crossing took a long time because the signal changed slowly. A small path through a park was shorter than the main road, but it became muddy after rain. They also found places where shade made walking comfortable in summer and corners where cars were difficult to see. The group decided to use symbols for these experiences. A blue mark showed a comfortable path, a red triangle showed a place that required care, and a green line showed a route with trees or shade. They walked the same route at different times and discovered that the experience changed. A quiet street in the morning became crowded when students returned home, while a sunny path became easier to walk in the late afternoon. When the maps were presented, each group had recorded different things. One group focused on wheelchair access, another on places where younger children might feel unsafe, and another on benches and public toilets. The teacher explained that maps are not neutral copies of reality. Every map selects information according to its purpose. A driving map, a disaster map, and a tourist map may show the same town in different ways because users need different information. Nana's group gave its walking map to the community center. A staff member said it could help new residents who wanted to explore the area without a car. Nana was proud, but she also understood the limits of their work. Their map represented only a few days and the experiences of a small group of students. Conditions could change with seasons, construction, or weather. The assignment taught her to ask two questions whenever she looked at a map: what information is included, and whose needs does it serve? She realized that understanding a place requires both a view from above and attention to what people experience on the ground.

The class later compared its walking maps with an official hazard map. Some comfortable routes crossed areas that were safe on ordinary days but could collect water during heavy rain. The students added a separate layer for emergency conditions instead of trying to combine every purpose into one map. Nana found this decision important. A route can be pleasant for a daily walk and still be a poor evacuation route. If all information is placed together without explanation, users may not know which feature matters at a particular moment. The class therefore added a short purpose statement at the top of each map. Nana learned that good information is not only accurate; it also tells the reader what question it is designed to answer.
translation:
奈々のクラスには少し変わった地理の課題が出ました。印刷された地図を見るだけでなく、地域を実際に歩き、『歩く人にとってどう感じる場所か』を示す地図を作るのです。最初は普通の地図と何が違うのか分かりませんでしたが、学校から図書館まで歩くと、地図にはない多くの情報に気づきました。橋の近くで歩道が急に狭くなる場所、信号待ちが長い横断歩道、近道だが雨の後はぬかるむ公園の道、夏に日陰が気持ちよい場所、車が見えにくい角などです。班は、歩きやすい道、注意が必要な場所、木陰のある道を色や記号で示しました。時間帯を変えて歩くと、朝は静かな道が下校時には混雑するなど、同じ場所でも状況が変わることも分かりました。発表では、車いす利用者の移動に注目した班、小さな子どもの安全を考えた班、ベンチや公衆トイレを記録した班など、それぞれ違う地図になりました。先生は、地図は現実をそのまま写すものではなく、目的に応じて情報を選んでいると説明しました。車用、防災用、観光用では同じ町でも必要な情報が異なります。奈々たちの地図は地域センターに渡され、新しい住民の散歩にも役立つと言われました。ただし奈々は、自分たちの地図も数日間の少人数の経験にすぎず、季節や工事、天気で変わるという限界にも気づきました。以来、地図を見るときには『何が載っているか』『誰の必要に応えるものか』を考えるようになりました。場所を理解するには、上から見る視点と、地上で人が感じる経験の両方が必要なのです。

クラスは歩行地図を防災地図とも比べました。普段は快適な道でも、大雨時には水がたまり避難には向かない場所がありました。そこで一枚に全部を詰め込まず、緊急時の情報を別の層として示しました。奈々は、正確な情報だけでなく『この地図は何の問いに答えるためのものか』を明示することが重要だと学びました。
